newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: IMF welcomes easier Swiss monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: IMF welcomes easier Swiss monetary policy.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Monday welcomed a Swiss shift to a looser monetary policy since mid-1995 as a step towards reviving the country's sluggish economy next year.

However, an IMF report cautioned that the Swiss National Bank must carefully balance between the risk of fuelling inflation with easier monetary policy and the danger of capping recovery by tightening future interest rates too soon.

An IMF team that spent the past week studying the Swiss economy estimated that real gross domestic product (GDP) would shrink by 0.5 percent this year and grow one percent in 1997, both levels broadly in line with recent forecast by Swiss economists.
The report noted that real GDP has been roughly flat in Switzerland since 1990, the longest stretch of real stagnation in the country's post-World War Two history.
"The stance of monetary policy has eased progressively since about mid-1995, although, with the benefit of hindsight, too cautiously," the IMF said.
"The recent reduction in the discount rate to one percent is, therefore, most welcome," the report added, referring to a 0.5-percentage point drop in that rate in September.
The Swiss National Bank began gradually lowering the discount rate in 1995 and began aggressivley adding liquidity to money markets in mid-1996 to spark economic growth.

The IMF report said the weakening since the rate cut of the Swiss franc against the German mark, the currency of Switzerland's biggest export market, indicated that monetery conditions were not tightening and probably easing further.
Recent easing of the Swiss franc would help boost exports, a key sector of the economy, the IMF said.
"The present constellation of exchange rates would not seem to pose an obstacle to a revival of growth, nor to be markedly inconsistent with fundamentals," it said.

The IMF said the present expansionary monetary stance should also help counter the dampening effect of long-term interest rates that were still high when measured by contemporaneous or projected inflation.
"Lower interest rates are also envisaged to help establish the pre-conditions for growth. Thus, domestic demand is forecast to experience some revival," the report added.
However, it said a looser money supply also bore longer term risks of fuelling inflation.

"Thus, the Swiss National Bank must carefully assess the unfolding situation to ensure that inflation is kept at an appropriately low level but also to avoid a premature tightening of monetary condition," the report said.
The IMF said inflation should continue at around one percent in 1997.
"One bleak spot, however, remains job creation, which is not expected to be sufficient to keep the unemployment rate from rising further in 1997," the IMF said.
